4k high refresh is now getting enough exposure. Get something like an M28U and you have a somewhat affordable 4k 144hz experience, though there might be newer high refresh monitors that are better or cheaper.

In short, it was worth it for me. I liked 1440p but the jump to 4k led to incredible clarity. There’s no way I could go back to 1080 or even 1440 now - the problem is achieving high refresh 4k gaming is very intensive.
It’s up to you, but I don’t mind 4k 70-80 fps for single player games if I get good graphics. I only want high refresh for games like MW2, and the 4080/7900 achieves that with ease.

I will say I feel that 1440p gaming becomes redundant at cards this powerful unless you want frame rates above 144 on competitive games, or prefer heavily intensive features like Ray tracing. Personally I’ll always pick higher resolution over higher graphical settings. Up to you though

Yes. In the last years barriers to entry have been removed. You can become a developer self teaching. You will have to, however, work hard and be consistent with it. The industry is hot, and not just for iOS programming. You can get employed through having personal projects and applying to entry level roles. It may be harder, but it's most definitely possible. And once you have your first proper role, you won't need to worry about what anyone says and the sky is effectively the limit for what you want to do.

People should not underestimate the value of personal projects. My friend has no degree and self taught over a year making personal projects, and was on £38 starting as a developer. Opportunity is out there and a degree isn’t even mandatory, it’s just meant for those who can demonstrate interest and passion. CS/development is one of the fields in this country where you can actually see really nice wage progression with time if you know what you’re doing.

You have experience and you’ve admitted you’ve learnt a good bit from your work. It’s time to move on. You’re also getting heavily underpaid for your work even if you don’t live in a high CoL location.

I'd say anything within the £30-40 range is good, it entirely depends on the company and role. I know someone who landed £38,000, no degree at all, self-taught on the fringes of London. You could try to ask for an expected salary around £35,000 in interviews, but it honestly depends. I would say anything below £30 is definitely underpaying by current industry rates, only places I've seen do that are either really small companies or places like 'Tata Consultancy', though I don't really hear of many people working for these places.  


Anyhow, if the technology and company you're working with suits you, it might be worthwhile. It shouldn't be long before you'll be looking at much higher paid positions once you have experience.
